title: Going backwards: how he learned scoring
summary: He describes backing into arranging, learning scoring from Goldkette and Whiteman, then technique in radio.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: To finish up with your career, I wanted to touch on the fact you said you had done teaching in recent years, and you mentioned that you studied the Schillinger method, and the way you put it was that you went backwards.
Well, I did. I would say I went backwards. When I got into this business and went with -- with those bands I told you about, the local bands -- and went

out playing my horn, and then I went away to college, and I had a band. Now, I sort of backed into writing. And then when I -- with the band the first year I'm out of college, I'm writing a little bit more, and I didn't know what it was all about to score. And then I got with the Goldkette band, and they taught me an awful lot.

And I rubbed elbows with I think, at the time, the greatest. And then from there on to the Whiteman band, although at this time, from the Goldkette band on, I learned how to score. Now then, after the Whiteman band, I got into the radio business, and there you have to know how -- by that time I had built up a certain amount of musical techniques that -- which you usually learn when you first start to go to school. You learn all these things, and you spend your first few days being a tyro, you know. So you -- you work hard at something like that.
And then by the time you get along out of a band like the Whiteman band or out of radio, you're ready for -- for Hollywood. You know, you go into something further.
